Dear Requester
Thank you for your recent correspondence which I am responding to on behalf of the Leader, concerning Great House Farm/Church View Close, the removal of a commemorative tree and your communications with Councillor Carroll.
I have considered the matters you have raised.
As you are aware, I have previously responded to your concerns regarding Councillor Carroll's lack of response to your correspondence. Having reviewed those concerns, I concluded that the matter did not fall within the Council's Corporate Complaints Policy and I did not identify any basis for further action under the Members' Code of Conduct process. The Council has no mechanism by which it can compel an elected member to respond to correspondence from a constituent and, accordingly, the Council's consideration of that aspect of the matter is concluded.
Please note that the Leader is not responsible for the conduct of Members other than those with her own political group
I note that your recent correspondence extends beyond the issue of Councillor Carroll's responsiveness and raises a broader range of concerns relating to historical land ownership, planning and heritage matters associated with Great House Farm/Church View Close, together with a request for information regarding the removal of a commemorative tree.
In relation to the tree, I am making enquiries to establish whether the Council holds any records which may assist in answering your question regarding its removal. This is being dealt with by the Information Governance Team, I have copied in the FOI unit email domain. If relevant information is held by the Council, I will advise you accordingly. Equally, if no such records are held, I will confirm that position.
In respect of the wider matters raised in your correspondence, it is important that I clarify the scope of the Council's role. The Council is not able to determine disputed ownership of land, revisit historical legal proceedings, adjudicate upon competing title █████, or investigate allegations of █████ or other criminal conduct. Those matters fall within the jurisdiction of the courts, HM Land Registry, the police and other external bodies as appropriate.
Whilst I appreciate the strength of feeling reflected in your correspondence and recognise the significance that these matters have for you and your family, the Council must limit its involvement to those issues which fall within its statutory functions and responsibilities. Any response provided by the Council will therefore be confined to matters upon which it may properly comment and any information which it may hold.
The FOI team will write to you further once enquiries regarding the tree have been completed.
Yours sincerely,

I write to you as Leader of the Vale of Glamorgan Council because the elected member for Llandough, Councillor George D. D. I understand that elected members do not have a line manager in the employment sense. Councillor Carroll is Leader of the Conservative Group. You are the political head of the authority. After the ward member and the Monitoring Officer, you are the proper next addressee.

Why I am writing to you rather than waiting further

1. Councillor Carroll has not sent a single substantive reply to me at █████<█████>.
2. On 27 July 2026 I filed a formal complaint about that silence (copied to him, Democratic Services and the Monitoring Officer).

That is a local enquiry a ward member can signpost to Parks, Highways, Planning or the landowner. It is not a request that he retry BP Properties Ltd v Buckler.

From his public output, Councillor Carroll appears to concentrate on blocked drains, potholes and similar highway defects. Those matters matter. The correspondence I sent him is of a different character: heritage, planning and enforcement records, the 1988 demolition of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), now Church View Close, and the removal of a commemorative tree. I accept that may be outside the type of casework he usually handles. That is why a short, honest reply — even if only to say the questions sit with named officers, and to pass the tree query to the correct department — would have been sufficient. Silence is not.

Recorded approaches to Councillor Carroll (█████<█████>)

- 4 May 2026 — follow-up on BP v Buckler 1987; ITV footage; request for attention as Llandough councillor.

- 9 May 2026 — a wider formal notice also addressed to █████<█████>. That address bounced. Subsequent mail used the correct gdcarroll@ address.
- 7 June 2026 — “Church View Close, Llandough”. 1988 events from public records, family █████ and media.

- 13 July 2026 — “Great House Farm / Church View Close”. Full timeline restated. Ten-working-day request. Explicit question: who removed the tree my great-grandfather planted to commemorate the ownership claim, as shown in the Collection of Wales archive image.
- 27 July 2026 — formal complaint to █████<█████>, copied to Councillor Carroll, Democratic Services and the Monitoring Officer.
- 28 August 2026 — further letter to Councillor Carroll and Stephen Doughty MP on the same site.

What I am asking you to do

1. Note that the ward member has not answered, and that the complaint process produced no requirement that he do so.

2. Ask Councillor Carroll, or the relevant Director, to provide a short written reply on the tree: which department or landowner authorised or carried out its removal, on what date, and under what power or works order — or to confirm that the Council holds no such record.

3. Identify the correct officer contact for heritage, trees and historic planning records at Church View Close / former Great House Farm, so I am not left circling a silent ward inbox.

4. Confirm whether the Council will treat a documented family connection to a demolished historic farmstead in the ward as a legitimate basis for a reply, even where the correspondent is not presently resident in Llandough.

The thesis of my concern is that the lawfare/ warfare that systematically attempted to make our occupancy permissive as early as the 40's (with my grandmothers statement of title being █████, a failed attempt to get us into a tenancy afterwards, and ambiguity in a 1955 order for another parcel we leased and defaulted on, which later meant it was able to be misinterpreted to make it appear our parcel of land (now Church View Close) was part of theirs, like it was in 1916 - 1928) is a racket. The ownership dispute was a problem created. The reaction followed and the solution was to focus on possession. And so in 1987 BP were awarded possession with what was a defective title chain.

I do not expect you to reopen 1987 litigation. I do expect the authority, once the ward member has been given months and a formal complaint, to answer a factual question about a tree on land in that ward. Because that tree was part of a long list of evidence supporting our ownership claim.

I can supply the original emails and the 27 July complaint in full if Democratic Services does not already have them. See attached the aforementioned tree planting ceremy image. I also enclose a draft chancery court allocation so you can understand the legal arguments.

Followed by ECHR rejection citing BP own the land, despite BP only seeking possession and never seeking or gaining ownership.

I have a trove of evidence and I am collecting more and investigating and in talks with CPS and █████ Police and MoJ and Land Registry. seeking these records is, however, a material chronology, particularly
because he had initially adopted a position of not engaging beyond a
statutory search. I therefore ask the Council to establish the facts rather
than assume either that the matter is innocuous or that any wrongdoing
occurred.

   1. Llandough Community Council records

In May and June 2026 I asked Mr Egan for Community Council records
concerning Great House Farm, including material concerning the events
surrounding my late father's involvement with the property in 1988.

On 14 June 2026 Mr Egan stated that minute books from 1982 onwards had been

subsequently retired. On the day of his retirement he directed me towards
Leckwith records and the 1939 Western Ground Rents tenancy with my
great-grandfather.

That tenancy is significant because, on the documents I have examined, it
appears to concern the eastern field rather than the House Plot containing
the farmhouse and associated buildings. I therefore do not regard that
reference as resolving the documentary position concerning Great House Farm
itself.

I need the Council to establish:

   - who is now Clerk and Proper Officer of Llandough Community Council;
   - who currently has custody of its historic minute books, correspondence
   and other records;
   - what records were handed over or inventoried when Mr Egan retired;
   - whether any search has been made specifically for Great House Farm /
   Tŷ Mawr records, rather than relying solely on the general statement that
   minute books were deposited in 2002; and
   - whether any Community Council correspondence, consultation response or
   minute relating to 89/01396/OUT or the later reserved matters survives.

If any part of this falls solely within the responsibility of Llandough
Community Council or the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales, please
identify the appropriate authority and the person to whom I should address
that part of the complaint.

   2. What the existing evidence establishes

This section turns from Community Council custody to the Vale's own
planning and archaeological file for 89/01396/OUT. The points below are
based on documents already in my possession and published archaeological
material, and are separate from the matters in Section 1, where I am asking
the Council to search its records.

   1.

   Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr is recorded in the historic environment
   record as County Treasure, reference SMR/HER 2038s / GGAT02038s, at
   approximately ST 1681 7331. The 1990 GGAT assessment records that, because
   of an ownership dispute and the subsequent sudden destruction of the
   property in 1988, the building was incompletely understood.
   2.

   Outline planning application 89/01396/OUT, submitted by BP Properties
   Ltd, followed the 1988 demolition by approximately a year. The application
   answers the relevant questions as follows: buildings to be demolished —
   "None"; site — "Disused"; previous use — "Not known".
   3.

   The Vale officer material in my possession refers to an outline-stage
   indicative scheme of 18 dwellings. The subsequent reserved-matters scheme
   approved on 3 September 1992 is for 20 dwellings.
   4.

   The 1990 evaluation recorded archaeological potential to the north of
   the churchyard and identified a medium-to-high potential area. What it does
   not establish by itself is the full extent of the archaeological remains
   subsequently encountered.
   5.

   Cotswold Archaeology excavated at the same general location in 1994,
   immediately adjacent to St Dochdwy's Church. The published archaeological
   account records 1,026 burials from an excavated area of 0.22 hectares. I am
   relying on the excavators' published figure rather than the lower secondary
   figure of 858, which appears to conflate different phases of investigation.
   6.

   PPG16 was issued in November 1990 and therefore post-dates the March
   1990 outline decision, but was applicable by the time of the September 1992
   reserved-matters decision. I am not presently asserting what archaeological
   conditions were imposed in 1992. The drawings I hold are stamped as
   approved on 3 September 1992, subject to compliance with conditions if any,
   but I do not hold the decision notice setting out the actual conditions.
   That decision notice is therefore a critical missing document.
   7.

   I am also not treating the handwritten numbering on the surviving
   consultation material as conclusively establishing which sheet relates to
   which responding body. The underlying consultation responses remain
   relevant and should be located irrespective of that numbering issue.
   8.

   The documentary gap that now needs explaining

The sequence is straightforward.

The historic farmhouse and associated buildings were demolished in December
1988.

The subsequent 1989 outline application described the site as "Disused",
stated that there were "None" buildings to be demolished, and gave the
previous use as "Not known".

The 1990 archaeological evaluation had already identified significant
archaeological potential near the churchyard.

The 1992 reserved-matters approval provided for 20 dwellings.

The 1994 excavation subsequently recorded 1,026 burials from 0.22 hectares
immediately adjacent to the church.

What I cannot establish from the records presently available to me is how
the archaeological excavation area relates spatially to the approved
housing layout and retained areas. In particular, I need the 1994
excavation plan and the corresponding Ideal Homes layout so that the two
can be compared accurately.

I also need to understand how the 1989 application descriptions came to be
accepted against the documentary and historic-environment information
already available concerning the demolished farmhouse.

I am not asking the Council to adopt my interpretation of these matters. I
am asking it to establish what was known, what was checked, what was
recorded, and what records still exist.

   4. Specific information and records requested

Please provide a substantive written response to each of the following:

   1.

   Who is currently Clerk and Proper Officer of Llandough Community
   Council, and who has custody of its historic records?
   2.

   Was Llandough Community Council consulted on application 89/01396/OUT
   and/or the subsequent reserved-matters application? If so, please provide
   the consultation requests, replies, minutes and associated correspondence,
   or confirm specifically that no such material is held.
   3.

   Please provide the full planning decision notice dated 3 September 1992,
   including all conditions, rather than the approved drawings alone.
   4.

   Please confirm whether Vale holds the 1994 Cotswold Archaeology
   site/excavation plans and the relevant Ideal Homes development layout
   plans. Please also confirm whether the Council has ever undertaken or
   commissioned a plan-to-plan comparison showing the excavation area against
   the approved development footprint.
   5.

   Please identify the officer or officers responsible for assessing the
   1989 application against the information then available concerning the 1988
   demolition and HER/SMR record 2038s, including the entries "None",
   "Disused" and "Not known".
   6.

   Please confirm what planning, enforcement, conservation/heritage,
   archaeological, consultation, photographic and correspondence records
   remain for the site and where they are presently held.
   7.

   Given the issues raised by my FOI/EIR correspondence and the corporate
   complaint of 17 September 2026, please ensure that surviving records
   concerning Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, including Community Council records
   where they remain identifiable, are preserved pending resolution of these
   matters. I am particularly concerned that records should not disappear
   simply because responsibility has passed from one office-holder to another.
   8.

   Please confirm whether there was a formal handover, inventory or records
   transfer when Mr Egan retired, and whether any such documentation records
   the location of material concerning Great House Farm, planning
   consultations, or the 1988 demolition.
   9.

   Finally, if the Council considers that any aspect concerning Mr Egan's
   conduct as Community Council Clerk falls outside the Vale's jurisdiction,
   please identify the proper route and responsible body rather than simply
   closing that part of the complaint.

I am deliberately separating evidence from inference. I am not alleging
that Mr Egan's retirement was caused by my FOI requests, nor am I alleging
that any individual deliberately concealed records. The timing, however, is
sufficiently relevant that the Council should establish what happened to
the records at the point responsibility changed. The immediate issue is
capable of being answered objectively: what records exist, what was known
to the authority, what checks were carried out, what decisions were made,
and where the missing documents are now.

Please treat this as a formal request for a written governance/records
response and address each numbered question individually. It should be read
alongside FOI/EIR reference 00210772 and my correspondence of 17–18
September 2026.

Regards,

Requester 

------------------------------

Changes made: added the Re: line, opened Section 2 with a sentence flagging
the shift from Community Council custody to the Vale's own file, and merged
the two closing paragraphs to drop the repeated point. Everything else —
including all the evidence/inference hedging — is untouched. Want it as a
Word doc or PDF instead, or any further tweaks?

*MP *Doughty,

Further to the correspondence from Mr Iain Banfield, and my earlier email,
I am writing again to be sure, placed on record, is the central issue which
HM Land Registry's response still does not answer.

I appreciate that HM Land Registry is not a court and that it cannot simply
reopen a Court of Appeal judgment. That, however, does not answer the
separate question of whether the land registered in 1982/83 was correctly
identified and supported by the documentary title then placed before the
Registrar.

Mr Banfield's response relies heavily upon *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler*
[1987] EWCA Civ 2. That judgment post-dated the registration by
approximately four years. It records BP Properties Ltd as having become
registered proprietor of the "whole farm" in November 1982 and then
determines the later adverse-possession dispute concerning the farmhouse
and garden. It does not, however, determine whether the 1982
first-registration application had itself correctly included the farmhouse
parcel in BP's documentary title, or whether the registration had
mistakenly conflated two historically separate parcels.

That distinction is fundamental.

My family's parcel — the former farmhouse, garden and curtilage, which I
refer to as the *House Plot* — was historically distinct from the adjoining
eastern agricultural land. The documentary history I have obtained
indicates that these areas were not simply one undifferentiated proprietary
parcel.

The 1916 agricultural tenancy is one important document because it embraced
both areas. But that is not the end of the conveyancing history. The
earlier 1877 Daniel Thomas & Son instrument, and the arrangement
subsequently acted upon when the quarrying ceased in 1928, point to a
separate proprietary interest in the House Plot.

I have the 1938 conveyance from the Marquis of Bute to Western Ground
Rents, and the revised 1939 version of the 1916 tenancy, and it did not
convey or demise the House Plot at all: the actual 1938 conveyance, the
1939 tenancy and their plans need to be examined by you lot too, not just
me. Indeed, the 1987 judgment itself records that the █████ yearly
tenancy commencing in 1949 has not been produced in the proceedings. Its
geographical extent therefore remains unproved. Not withstanding it may
pertain to the parcel to the east we leased and defaulted on, not our
freehold parcel. Furthermore my nan expressly rejected the 1949 tenancy and
attempt to make her occupancy of our parcel permissive in such a way, but
expressly rejecting it while asserting her ownership claim of her parcel.

It's adolescent of everyone to keep having a meltdown and failing to
compute the simplicity of the fact Mary Williams asserted she owned her
parcel. And WGR saught possession of theirs, east of it. Western Ground
Rents, already described in UK Parliament as praying on elderly and being
abhorrent and scrupilous, clearly tried to make Mary's occupany appear
permissive in 1949 and the 1955  proceedings.

The 1987 judgment records that and the 1962 proceeding, after the
agricultural tenancy was terminated, as Western Ground Rents obtaining a
1955 possession order for the "whole of the farm". Crucially, however, when
that order was enforced on 4 July 1955, possession was taken of all
parts *except
the farmhouse and garden*. The judgment gives the immediate reason as Mrs
Mary Buckler's condition and her strong resistance to leaving the
farmhouse. Ambiguity which is later misinterprited and clearly an early
attempt at making her occupancy of her parcel appear permissive.

WGR subsequently brought a *fresh action in 1962 specifically against Mr
and Mrs  Buckler for possession of the farmhouse and garden and mesne
profits*, resulting in the possession and mesne-profits order of 11
December 1962. The judgment records that this order was not enforced before
1974.

That sequence matters.

If the two areas had genuinely always constituted one undifferentiated
proprietary estate subject to the same right of possession, it is difficult
to understand why possession of the agricultural land was recovered in 1955
while the farmhouse and garden were left occupied and a separate possession
action had to be brought in 1962.

I therefore ask that this fact not be retrospectively converted into an
assumption that the 1955 "whole farm" wording necessarily comprised the
House Plot in the same legal sense as the agricultural land.

The statutory effect attributed by the Court of Appeal to the 1955/1962
proceedings cannot itself establish title to a different, historically
separate parcel which was never actually comprised in those proceedings.

The possession orders were orders for possession and associated relief.
They were not conveyances. They did not retrospectively create a
documentary chain of title where none existed, nor did they by themselves
determine the geographical extent of an underlying freehold documentary
title.

That is especially important in light of the sequence of events recorded in
the 1987 judgment. WGR's own successive proceedings and selective
enforcement distinguished the agricultural land from the farmhouse and
garden in practical terms, whatever the later interpretation of the
expression "whole farm".

There is a further point which I believe HM Land Registry has not addressed.

In 1949, █████ the history now being assembled, Mrs Mary Williams
was offered a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden which she rejected
because she asserted ownership. The 1987 judgment itself confirms that she
was offered a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden by Western Ground Rents
and refused it. It also records that she had come to believe she had a
title through her grandfather and that documents existed which supported
that claim.

Thus there was plainly a known dispute over the House Plot long before
first registration.

The 1974 proceedings and letters must also be put in their proper place.
The Court of Appeal held that the 1974 letters operated as a licence,
notwithstanding that Mrs Buckler had never expressly accepted them, and
held that her possession thereafter was no longer adverse.

I am not asking HM Land Registry to disregard that decision.

Despite it being clear to any sane, reasonable person to see that, given
the evidence, the 1974 order was not truly quashed due to the licence
letters, which came afterwards and were backdated. Made out to a non
existent Mrs Buckler. And quashed the case within minutes of Mary being
notified of them, with no ample opportunity to respond. Albeit she actually
did in writing. And asserted her ownership and challenged BP in a public
newspaper. Not withstanding BP couldn't give something they don't own i.e.
permissive occupancy.

This permissive occupancy followed by a conversion is a racket. Look at the
pattern;

1955 permissive occupancy ploy > 1969 conveyance (WGR to BP Pension Trust
Ltd)

1974 permissive occupancy ploy > 1975 conveyance (BP Pension Trust to BP
Properties Ltd)

Nor am I asking the Land Registry to even acknowledge the fact court
clerked notified the press who all decended on the scene, covered the story
(that Mary asserted ownership, family occupancy since 1667, lawyer confirms
her ownership claim was valid etc).

I am asking a different question: *what land did BP actually have title to
in 1974, and what land was actually capable of being registered in BP's
name in 1982?*

If the House Plot had never formed part of WGR's documentary estate (not in
the 1938 conveyance from Bute, as it went to Daniel Thomas & Son in 1876
then to my great grandad John Williams in 1928), then the 1974 letters and
the 1962 possession order cannot simply be assumed to cure that problem.
The 1987 judgment did not adjudicate that separate issue of
first-registration procedure and documentary extent.

BP never had ownership. Ours ownership claim was never legally
exstiguished. BP never even saught ownership, only possession. And with no
title chain, only their own issuance of permissive occupancy, based on
interest they'd purchased in a possession order, which itself was also
based on issuance of permissive occupancy. And with little to no meeting of
the minds, but instead stealth/ secrecy. And the registration itself in
1983 was secret and undisclosed to Mary Williams and us living heirs and
successors.
The Land Registry issue

The applicable statutory framework in 1982/83 was the Land Registration Act
1925 and the Land Registration Rules 1925.

The Rules expressly contained provisions dealing with first registration,
including *rule 20, requiring the applicant to deliver the original deeds
and documents relating to the title which were in its possession or control*.
The operation of that rule in the first-registration context is confirmed
in *Walker v Burton*, where the High Court described the requirement in
those terms.

The Rules also contained a specific provision headed *"Examination of title
by Registrar"* and provisions concerning searches and enquiries by the
Registrar.

This means that the question cannot simply be reduced to "Land Registry
registers what it is given".

The relevant question is whether, in this case:

   1.

   the applicant supplied the material title documents in its possession or
   control;
   2.

   the documents supplied actually demonstrated that the House Plot formed
   part of the estate being registered;
   3.

   the Registrar examined the documentary chain sufficiently to identify
   any inconsistency between the deeds and the land claimed for registration;
   4.

   any discrepancy between the deeds, plans, possession orders and the
   proposed registration plan generated a requisition or further enquiry;
   5.

   the registration was completed as an absolute title despite a material
   uncertainty as to the extent of the documentary title; and
   6.

   the Registrar's own records contain any warning, requisition, note,
   correspondence or other indication that the separate House Plot issue was
   considered.

There is a particularly important point concerning *registration in error*.

The Law Commission's review of the 1925 system records that the Land
Registration Rules 1925 contained a specific power in *rule 14* dealing
with "registration in error", including registration of too large a part of
a title, and explained that the registrar had an express power to rectify
registration arising from mistake.

That is significant because HM Land Registry is currently saying, in
effect, that there was no mistake. That conclusion should not be treated as
established unless HM Land Registry has actually examined the surviving
1982/83 registration file and established what documentary evidence
justified the extent registered.

HM Land Registry's present published guidance also expressly recognises
that *including too much land in a registered title can constitute a
mistake in the register*, and gives as an example a title being mapped to
include land for which the registered proprietor has no documentary title.
It also recognises that failure by a solicitor to lodge documents in their
possession can amount to lack of proper care. I appreciate that this is
modern guidance and I do not suggest that it can simply be imposed
retrospectively as the law of 1983. It is nevertheless directly relevant to
the distinction HM Land Registry now draws between a genuine registration
mistake and a mere disagreement about the title boundary.

Likewise, HM Land Registry's current guidance states that a title plan
cannot describe the land more accurately than the pre-registration deeds
allow, and that the pre-registration deeds are crucial to resolving
questions about the extent of a registered title. Again, I cite this as an
expression of the documentary basis of registration, not as a claim that a
2025/26 practice guide was itself the governing rule in 1983.
The present register raises further questions
In addition to reperations for the demolition of our 800 year old home with
us practically still inside at the time, inhumane abuse of my pregnant mum,
terminally ill father and amputee grandmother, not withstanding 3 toddlers:
myself included. I seek restoration of property in that I seek possession
of the undeveloped woodland half of our land parcel. Which is virgin land,
having not been touched since we were forced from it in 1988.

The current title material itself refers separately to:

   - the *23 May 1975 conveyance of land tinted blue*, with the copy plan
   filed under *WA240304*;
   - the *19 November 1982 conveyance of land tinted pink*, with the
   original filed under *WA231076*;
   - rights and retained land associated with those separate conveyances;
   and
   - the vendors' adjoining or retained land.

Those entries require the original plans to be compared with the House Plot.

I am particularly concerned that two separate conveyancing areas were
subsequently presented as part of a single "whole farm" registered estate.
If the House Plot was not actually comprised in the conveyances relied
upon, the relevant question is not whether the modern red edging can be
made to fit an Ordnance Survey map. The question is *what deed, order or
other legally sufficient evidence put that specific land into BP's
registrable estate in the first place*.

An Ordnance Survey description cannot by itself create a conveyance. Much
like BPs 1971 alteration of the descriptor of our parcel, shifting "ty
mawr" from theirs to ours and appending "farm" to the end of it.

Nor can a later registration description retrospectively supply a missing
link in the pre-registration conveyancing chain.

I'll repeat this as its important;

Nor can a later registration description retrospectively supply a missing
link in the pre-registration conveyancing chain.
The 1982/83 registration file

HM Land Registry's letter of *30 July 2026, reference N610CGV*, has already
confirmed that surviving first-registration material relating to the
relevant titles exists and is open to inspection.

I therefore ask you to write again to HM Land Registry, not asking it to
decide the family title, but asking it to answer the following precise
administrative questions:

*1.* What exact first-registration applications were made for *WA231076*
and *WA240304*, and what deeds, abstracts, declarations, plans, court
orders and other documents accompanied each application?

*2.* Did the application files contain the *1938 Bute–Western Ground Rents
conveyance*, the *1939 revised tenancy and plan*, *1877 Daniel Thomas & Son
instrument*, or any other document showing that the House Plot was
historically separate? What was included and not included.

*3.* What document was relied upon to establish that the House Plot formed
part of BP Properties Limited's documentary estate? How was Land Registry
not able to see only a plaintiff on the court paperwork preceeding 1982,
and no defendant?

*4.* What was the precise geographical extent attributed to the 1955
possession order and the 1962 possession order by the Registrar, and were
the original orders or plans ever examined?

*5.* Were the Registrar's records aware of the 1974 proceedings and Mrs
Williams  asserted ownership claim when the first-registration applications
were processed?

The only way they could have not been is if they willfully ignorantly and
selective vision didn't see there was another party to the court
proceedings, not just a claimant but also a defendant. They/ BP will have
had to have fished out a 1935 marriage certificate to find anything to
match the name Mrs Buckler, on the licence letters. A deperate measure to
avoid any of this clandestine registration reaching the families knowledge,
which we would have been very quick to correct all this. Not withstanding
my nan will have had to have died to not challenge this, having
relentlessly and unwaveringly challenged this for decades already. And low

*6.* Did the Registrar raise any requisition because the possession

*7.* On what evidence was the House Plot incorporated into the land

What I am asking you to investigate

I am not asking you, or HM Land Registry, to determine that my family is

I am asking that the Department distinguish between two entirely different

*First:* the Court of Appeal decided the legal effect of the 1962

*Second:* HM Land Registry registered land in BP's name in 1982/83. That
administrative act necessarily depended upon a first-registration
application, documentary evidence and a determination of the land capable
of registration.

The second proposition cannot simply be proved by citing the first.

If HM Land Registry now asserts that there was no mistake in registration,
it should be able to identify the documentary chain and the registration
evidence which led it to that conclusion.

Is land registry claiming my great grandad John Williams DID NOT gain and
register title, in 1928, when the 1876/77 Marquess of Bute to Daniel Thomas
and Son agreement enacted, thus title chain/ freehold transferred from DT&S

If the surviving file shows that the House Plot was supported by a valid

If, however, the file shows that the House Plot was included because an

I am deliberately not asserting █████ or negligence as an established fact

Evidence must establish what happened. But the possibility of *administrative

That is precisely why I am asking for the surviving file to be reviewed.

I remain willing to provide the title extracts, the 30 July 2026 HM Land

MP Doughty,

Further to my letter earlier, I would like to narrow what I am kindly
asking of you, and to correct one other thing.

My letter asked which document brought the former farmhouse and garden at
Great House Farm into BP Properties Limited's registrable estate. HM Land
Registry has in fact already answered that, and I should have acknowledged
it. Its letters of 23 March and 19 April 2026 identify a conveyance dated
19 November 1982 for title WA231076, and a conveyance dated 23 May 1975 for
title WA240304. I will apply to HM Land Registry directly, on form OC2, for
copies of those deeds and their plans. I am not asking you to obtain them
for me.

Two questions remain. Both concern inconsistencies within HM Land
Registry's own correspondence, rather than anything I am asserting. So that
you need not open any attachments, I have set out the relevant passages
verbatim in the annex below, with dates and authors.

1. The 1971 abstract of title. The letter of 19 April 2026 states twice
that an abstract of title dated 1971 was lodged with the applications. The
letter of 30 July 2026 sets out a complete schedule of the documents held
on both first-registration files — thirty items for WA231076 and thirteen
for WA240304 — and no abstract of title appears anywhere on either list.
Was the abstract lodged; does the list of documents lodged (item 17 on that
schedule) record it; and if it was lodged, what became of it?

2. The conveyance of 31 December 1969. Both operative conveyances recite
the same root of title: a conveyance dated 31 December 1969 between Western
Ground Rents Limited and The British Petroleum Pension Trust Limited. That
deed does not appear on the 30 July schedule either. Was it produced to the
registry at first registration; does the list of documents lodged record
it; and if it was not produced, on what evidence was the recital accepted
as establishing the root of title?

Both questions can be answered by examining a single document which HM Land
Registry confirms it holds and describes as open to public inspection. I am
not asking it to reopen BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, to
determine ownership, or to revisit any decision it has made. A written
answer to those two questions is all I am seeking.

I can also withdraw one request from my earlier letter. I asked that the
surviving records be preserved; that is no longer necessary, as HM Land
Registry has confirmed the documents will remain on file.

My earlier request to meet you stands, but it is not pressing. These two
questions can be dealt with in writing.

Yours sincerely,

Requester

PS - see attached images. I purchased all deeds I could, but the primary
one is inaccessible for purchase as of today. I have raised this issue with
A.I.

On the standard applied:

"In unregistered conveyancing, title is ultimately based on the estate
owner's right to be in possession of the land or to receive the rents and
profits of it. Showing a full documentary title commencing with a good root

On the abstract of title, in relation to WA240304:

On the root of title recited in the 19 November 1982 conveyance:

"The recitals clause (preamble) to that Conveyance states 'The Vendors are

Mawr, Llandough, I attach a formal schedule of the records I am seeking, so
that the request is easier for Heneb to work through and to allocate

a chaser. It is to put the detail in one place and to clarify the basis of
the request.

On your note of 22 May. You are right that Heneb, as a limited company, is
not a public authority under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, and I do
not pursue that. Two separate points remain, and I would welcome Heneb's
position on each.

First, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 apply on a different
test — regulation 2(2) reaches bodies carrying out functions of public
administration relating to the environment, or under the control of a
public authority. If Heneb considers it falls outside that, please say so
expressly with brief reasons, so that I can direct the request elsewhere.

Second, and independently, the Historic Environment Record is a statutory
record: sections 194 and 195 of the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023
require the Welsh Ministers to maintain an HER for every local authority
area and to make it available for public inspection, and Heneb keeps the
south-east Wales record on their behalf. I therefore ask in the alternative
that this be treated as a request for access under that regime and under
Heneb's own policy.

Two things that will make this easier. If any item is too broad, please
tell me which and I will narrow it rather than have the whole request
refused. And if Heneb can supply, as a first step, simply a schedule or
index of the records it holds for this site — without copying them — that
would let me target the rest precisely and save your staff considerable
time. I am content to inspect material by appointment at Baglan or at the
HER, and any reasonable copying or staff-time charge can be notified to me
in advance for approval.

Two small administrative points. Please confirm which legal entity now
holds the records and functions formerly of Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological
Trust Ltd, and who within Heneb handles access requests of this kind.

Finally, since my correspondence in May was framed more formally: my
purpose is documentary. I am reconstructing the record of a farm my family
occupied for generations, and I would far rather do that with Heneb's help
than around it.

I should say plainly that I have read GGAT's December 1993 notification to

site files and correspondence files in the 1980s and today, and
confirmation whether any records relating to this site have been destroyed
under it, and if so when and under what authority.

or retention from, The National Archives or the Glamorgan Archives**, and
the outcome of any such review.
> 7. All **Inventory working papers, drafts, card-index entries and record
cards** for the site, including those for Glamorgan Inventory site 425.

transparencies, digital images, and any oblique or vertical aerial coverage

their catalogue entries. Given Suggett's 1988 note that there is apparently
no photographic record, **please state expressly whether the Commission
holds none**, and whether any images sit within RCS2/1/1777 or in
uncatalogued Emergency Recording material.

inside **RCS2/1/1777**, whether that bundle is Bonvilston or Llandough. If
Llandough, please re-link it to NPRN 20182 and supply a contents list and
copies. Please also check adjacent case **RCS2/1/1776**. *(This is my
request of 15 September, restated here for completeness only — it stands on
its own date.)*
> 10. Any record of a site visit, watching brief, recording exercise or
emergency recording carried out or considered before, during or after the
demolition; any notification of the proposed demolition, from whom and on
what date; and any decision **not** to record the building together with
the reasons recorded for it. The building was not listed — Cadw inspected
on 29 July 1988 and did not list it — so I make no assumption that the
Commission was entitled to notice. What I would like to know is what the

reports of 3 December 1988 stated that Cadw was considering emergency
listing and that discussion with the Commission was being arranged. The

elevations, published or unpublished.

continuation sheet, annotation and enclosure — not only the passages
concerning the c.1880 find.
> 13. Any record of the source of the statement that the c.1880 ironwork

confirms, corrects or withdraws that attribution.
> 14. All correspondence between the Commission and any of the following

Cymru; any Member of Parliament; and any member of my family.

GGAT, Cadw, Cotswold Archaeology or any other body relating to this site.

link is enough **provided** you confirm the online record is complete. If
any item is held elsewhere — The National Archives, Glamorgan Archives,
Cadw, Heneb or Amgueddfa Cymru — please name the body and reference so I

the internal review procedure, so that I know where to direct any review
request if one becomes necessary.
>
> With thanks for your patience with a long list.
>
> Yn gywir / Yours faithfully,
>
> Requester
> █████

Wigley,

I sent you the formal complaint below on 17 September 2026. I have since
established that it never reached you.

It was addressed to █████, which rejected it — my mail server
recorded "message blocked… the address couldn't be found or is unable to
receive email." A copy addressed to █████ also failed, that
domain having been decommissioned. The only addresses that accepted it were
█████ and █████.

The latter is Cadw's visitor-services contact centre operated by Transport
for Wales, which replied on 18 September under reference #628635887 to say
it had been passed to their complaints manager. That is plainly not the
right destination for a complaint about a 1988 listing assessment, and I do
not want it pursued there. I would be grateful if that reference could be
closed.
I should add that █████ has now rejected correspondence from me on
three separate occasions — 23 January, 29 August and 17 September 2026. If
that address is still published anywhere as a contact point for Cadw, it
may be worth someone looking at.

I am therefore re-serving the complaint on you directly, unchanged. The
text below is exactly as sent on 17 September. Please treat it as received
today, and please let me have a complaint reference.

Two points of clarification, so that nothing is misread.

First, this is not a further Freedom of Information request. I accept your
email of 4 September, in which you confirmed that Cadw has released all the
records it holds concerning the 1988 listing decision, and I am not asking
you to produce documents you have already said no longer survive. I am
conscious that I have made requests to Cadw and to the Welsh Government
Information Rights Unit since May of this year and that they have been
answered. My complaint is not that records are being withheld. It is about
what can properly be established from the evidence that does survive, and
about whether Cadw's account distinguishes clearly enough between "we
cannot now establish this" and "this did not happen."

Second, I am treating this as stage one of the Welsh Government complaints
process, not stage two. You directed me to that process on 4 September. I
have copied the Complaints Advice Team so that the complaint is logged and
dated, but I am not asking for a formal investigation yet. I would rather
Cadw had the first opportunity to answer it. I will only escalate if the
stage one response does not engage with the ten matters set out at section
7 below.

One further matter, which I raise in the hope it is useful rather than as
part of the complaint. Cadw's 1988 file is lost, but Cadw did not
correspond with itself. Any letters Cadw wrote in 1988 about this building
were received by the Royal Commission, by Vale of Glamorgan Borough
Council, and by the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust, and copies may
survive in their files even though yours have gone. I have requests with
the Royal Commission and with Heneb which cover exactly that. If either
produces Cadw correspondence you no longer hold, I will send it to you, as
I said I would in August. I would rather Cadw's own record of this was
complete than score a point off its being incomplete.

I look forward to a complaint reference and to a substantive reply.

Yours sincerely,

Requester

Freedom of Information Officer,

Case Ref: 00211463 — request received 17 September 2026

I write to clarify and refine the above request while it remains open,
having now examined the original manuscript of the planning officer's
report rather than a transcription. My earlier request named two
organisations; the document in fact identifies the correspondents
differently, and I ask that the request be read as follows.

The passage relied upon
The planning officer's report on application 89/01396/OUT (residential
development including new access road, land at Great House Farm, Leckwith
Road, Llandough, Penarth; outline permission granted 13 March 1990) states,
at page 2:

"Two letters have been received from the Barry Preservation Society and
Civic Trust and a local County Councillor (who is a member of the Glamorgan
Gwent Archaeological Trust) making representations in respect of this
application and a copy of both these letters are attached to this report as
Appendices 'C' and 'D' respectively."

The following paragraph of the same report states:

"The Applicants' Agents have written in response to the report of the
Glamorgan Gwent Archaeological Trust Ltd. on the site and a copy of this
letter is attached to this report as Appendix 'E'."

What I request
Appendix "C" to the officer's report on 89/01396/OUT — the letter from the
Barry Preservation Society and Civic Trust.

Appendix "D" — the letter from the local County Councillor referred to,
together with that Councillor's name.

Appendix "E" — the letter from the Applicants' Agents responding to the
report of the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust Ltd.

A list of all appendices ("A" to "E" or further) to that officer's report,
so that the complete annex set is identified.

Any register, index, schedule or file list for application 89/01396/OUT
recording the documents originally held on the file.
A further document referred to in the same report

The officer's report also records, of the East Vale Local Plan:

"The greater part of the land is allocated for new residential development
in the East Vale Local Plan (Policy No. H.2.) The information supporting
the policy states that buildings on the site should be retained, however
were unfortunately demolished a little while ago."

I therefore also request:
The text of Policy H.2 of the East Vale Local Plan and the supporting
information to that policy referred to above, in the version current in
1989–1990.

Points on handling
These are documents the Council's own report states were attached to it. If
any of them is not held, I ask the Council to say so expressly, and to
state (a) when it ceased to be held, (b) under what retention schedule or
disposal decision, and (c) whether any record of that disposal exists. A
response that "no additional information has been identified" would not
address a request for annexes that the Council's own report records as
attached.

I note the Council's letter of 11 September 2026 in a related matter, which
stated that "further historical documentation has been found... not
necessarily Council documentation but is nonetheless in the Council's
possession". I ask that this material be searched in responding to the
present request.

I intend this as a clarification and refinement of case 00211463 under the
Council's duty to advise and assist (s.16 FOIA 2000 / reg. 9 EIR 2004), and
not as a new request. If the Council takes the view that any part of it
must be treated as a fresh request, please confirm that in writing,
identify which parts, and give the revised due date, so that I am not left
uncertain which deadline applies to which element.
I should be grateful for confirmation of receipt.

Regards,

Requester

Dr Misra,

Thank you for replying, and for doing so promptly and at a weekend. Good
drills Sir. What an honour. I know you and the Council serve as volunteers,
and I am grateful for the time.

Let me set out plainly what I am asking of the Council, which is narrow. If
you'll allow me?

I am not asking your Council to revisit Mr Egan's answer of 14 June 2026.
He explained that the minute books from 1982 onwards were deposited with
Glamorgan Archives in 2002, and I am pursuing those there.

What I am asking about is what that answer did not cover. Llandough
Community Council is a public authority under Schedule 1, Part II,
paragraph 7(b) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. The Act applies to
the recorded information set out below generally; the Environmental
Information Regulations 2004 apply in addition to any part of it that is
environmental information.

PART ONE — REQUEST FOR RECORDED INFORMATION

1. Whether the Council holds any recorded information created after the
2002 deposit — minutes, correspondence, reports, emails, photographs or
files of any kind — concerning Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) / Church View
Close, the village green in front of St Dochdwy's including registered
green VG 41, or the roadside verge by the churchyard wall.

2. Whether the Council holds any photographs, postcards or images of the
farm, the barn, the green or the church surroundings, of any date.

3. Whether the Council holds any recorded information showing what, if
anything, transferred to it from Penarth Town Council at the 1982
reorganisation, and any recorded information identifying where the pre-1982
Llandough community records were deposited.

If the answer to any of these is that no such information is held, I would
be content with a short statement to that effect — but I do need it stated.
Section 1(1)(a) of the Act requires the Council to confirm or deny whether
the information is held.

Section 10 (and regulation 5 of the EIR) allows twenty working days from
receipt, which on my request of 20 September 2026 I calculate as 16 October
2026.

If the Council is refusing, section 17 (and regulation 14) requires a
written refusal notice identifying the exemption or exception relied on;
section 17(7) requires the Council to give particulars of any complaints
procedure it operates, or to state that it has none, and to notify me of my
right to apply to the Information Commissioner; and regulation 11 gives a
right to an internal review of any refusal under the EIR.

"We have nothing more to add" does not meet those requirements. If the
period passes without a compliant response I will have no option but to
complain to the Information Commissioner.

PART TWO — MATTERS FOR THE COUNCIL'S DISCRETION

These are not part of the request above and carry no deadline. They are
simply things I would be grateful for.

A. I am not asking for the name or contact details of any individual. I am
asking whether the Council would be willing to pass my details to any
former member, former clerk or long-standing resident who might remember
the village between the 1950s and the 1990s, leaving it entirely to them
whether to contact me. I appreciate the Council may have data protection or
administrative reasons for declining, and I would not press it.

B. Whether the Council would be willing to table this correspondence at a
meeting and minute it. I am content for it to be tabled in full.

C. Whether the Council would consider, in due course, whether an
interpretation board or a plaque near the green would be appropriate. The
excavation on the land beneath Church View Close recorded 1,026 burials,
described in the published report as by far the largest early medieval
burial population so far recovered from Wales, above a Roman villa and an
Iron Age roundhouse. That history belongs to Llandough as much as to my
family, and there is nothing on the ground that records it. I would be glad
to give the Council or the community a short talk on the documentary
record, without charge, if that would be useful.

I should be grateful for a response to items 1 to 3 by 16 October 2026.

Regards,

Requester

Dear Rhodri, dear colleagues,
>
> Diolch am eich cydnabyddiaeth ar 8 Medi. On the Welsh Language Standards point raised in your signature — I am Welsh and I would be glad to receive correspondence in Welsh, but please use whichever language is quicker for you. I do not want language to delay anything, and I will not treat a Welsh reply as needing translation.
>
> This is a request under section 1 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, so far as the records concern the historic environment, under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.
>
> **First, a point of housekeeping. Nothing in this email amends, clarifies, narrows or withdraws my requests of 8, 15 or 17 September.** Those stand exactly as made and their statutory periods run from their own dates. This is an additional request, and I would not want it to be treated as restarting any clock. On my reckoning:
>
> - **8 September 2026** — FOI/EIR on R. F. Suggett's December 1988 unpublished records, H. J. Thomas's 1974 survey, the source of the "held by the National Museum of Wales" attribution, and copy correspondence with Amgueddfa Cymru, GGAT, Cadw and the Vale. Acknowledged by you the same day, twenty working days. **Due Tuesday 6 October 2026.** No reference number issued; nothing yet supplied.

> - **17 September 2026** — whether the Commission was notified, consulted or asked to record the farmhouse before its demolition on 6 December 1988. **Due Thursday 15 October 2026.**
>
> The second and third received only the automated enquiry acknowledgement, which cites fifteen working days and notes that the priority search service is suspended. I understand the staffing position and I am not complaining about it. But both emails ask for recorded information, and a request for recorded information is a request under section 1 whether or not it is labelled as one. **Please confirm that all three are logged as FOIA / EIR requests and let me have the reference numbers.** If they are currently sitting in the research-enquiry queue rather than the information-rights queue, that is easily fixed now and much harder to fix later.
>
> **On the number of requests.** I am conscious that this is my fifth email in twelve days. It is not an attempt to burden the Commission. Each request arose from a document I only found after sending the last one — the GGAT 1990 assessment led me to Suggett, Suggett's own note led me to the lost correspondence, and a Coflein search led me to RCS2/1/1777. I am content for all of them to be answered together in a single response if that is more efficient for you, and if the whole exceeds the appropriate limit under section 12 I will happily tell you which items to do first rather than have anything refused outright. Please just ask.
>
> **The site.** Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough (Llandochau) juxta Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan — the community of St Dochdwy's Church and Llandough Hospital. **Not** Llandough near Cowbridge, and **not** Ty Mawr, Bonvilston (Cadw 13603), which is a different and still-standing house. NPRN 20182. ST 1681 7331. HER GGAT02038s. Now Church View Close. Outbuildings demolished 30 November 1988; farmhouse 6 December 1988.
>
> Holdings I am aware of include file references **NA/GL/88/49** and **NA/GL/89/208**, NMR site file material catalogued on Coflein (a plan with additions dated 12 December 1988, a descriptive account, a press cutting), Inventory working papers for Glamorgan Inventory site 425, and the disputed ERC bundle RCS2/1/1777.
>
> **Why this matters to me.** The farm was my family's. The immediate reason for this request is a line in your own records: R. F. Suggett's December 1988 assessment notes that *"Correspondence between C. N. Johns and Mrs Buckler, Great House Farm, has been lost from the file since 1986/87"*, and that *"There is apparently no photographic record of the site."* Mrs Buckler was my relative. I want the correspondence if it survives, the record of how it came to be lost if it does not, and the rest of the file either way. I am not asking the Commission for a view on title or on the legality of the demolition, and I would not expect one.
>
> **Information requested**
>
> Please supply copies, so far as held:
>
> 1. A full contents list or file schedule for **NA/GL/88/49** and **NA/GL/89/208**, itemising every document on each file, whether or not the documents themselves are disclosed.
> 2. Copies of all documents on those two files.
> 3. **The file cover, front sheet or wrapper of each file**, and any enclosure list, loans register, issue slip, reader-request record or file-tracking entry attached to or kept for them.
> 4. Every record concerning the **C. N. Johns / Mrs Buckler correspondence** recorded as lost since 1986/87: any surviving copy, draft, extract, summary, index entry or catalogue stub; any contemporaneous or later note of its loss; any record of a search for it; any record of who consulted, borrowed or handled the file between 1 January 1985 and 31 December 1988; and any internal or external correspondence about its absence. If no such record exists, please say so expressly rather than leaving it unaddressed.
> 5. The Commission's **retention and disposal schedule** applicable to site files and correspondence files in the 1980s and today, and confirmation whether any records relating to this site have been destroyed under it, and if so when and under what authority.
> 6. Whether the files listed above have been **reviewed for transfer to, or retention from, The National Archives or the Glamorgan Archives**, and the outcome of any such review.
> 7. All **Inventory working papers, drafts, card-index entries and record cards** for the site, including those for Glamorgan Inventory site 425.
> 8. All **photographs** of the site in any format — prints, negatives, transparencies, digital images, and any oblique or vertical aerial coverage of Llandough showing the farm at any date — whether or not catalogued, with their catalogue entries. Given Suggett's 1988 note that there is apparently no photographic record, **please state expressly whether the Commission holds none**, and whether any images sit within RCS2/1/1777 or in uncatalogued Emergency Recording material.
> 9. Confirmation, from the location plan, map copies and photographs inside **RCS2/1/1777**, whether that bundle is Bonvilston or Llandough. If Llandough, please re-link it to NPRN 20182 and supply a contents list and copies. Please also check adjacent case **RCS2/1/1776**. *(This is my request of 15 September, restated here for completeness only — it stands on its own date.)*
> 10. Any record of a site visit, watching brief, recording exercise or emergency recording carried out or considered before, during or after the demolition; any notification of the proposed demolition, from whom and on what date; and any decision **not** to record the building together with the reasons recorded for it. The building was not listed — Cadw inspected on 29 July 1988 and did not list it — so I make no assumption that the Commission was entitled to notice. What I would like to know is what the Commission's own criteria for initiating Emergency Recording were at the time, and whether this site was considered against them. Contemporary reports of 3 December 1988 stated that Cadw was considering emergency listing and that discussion with the Commission was being arranged. The house came down three days later.
> 11. The **1974 survey by H. J. Thomas**, his site notes of 26 April 1974 and 12 December 1988, and any measured drawings, sketches, plans or elevations, published or unpublished.
> 12. **R. F. Suggett's December 1988 records in full** — every page, card, continuation sheet, annotation and enclosure — not only the passages concerning the c.1880 find.
> 13. Any record of the source of the statement that the c.1880 ironwork "is held by the National Museum of Wales", and any later file that confirms, corrects or withdraws that attribution.
> 14. All correspondence between the Commission and any of the following concerning this site, 1970–1995: Cadw or the Welsh Office; the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust; Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council; BP Properties Limited or its agents, including Debenham Tewson & Chinnocks; Persimmon Homes (Wales) Limited; Ideal Homes Wales Limited; Amgueddfa Cymru; any Member of Parliament; and any member of my family.
> 15. Any accession records for material deposited with the Commission by GGAT, Cadw, Cotswold Archaeology or any other body relating to this site.
>
> **Practicalities.** Please reply by email to this address. I cannot attend in person and I am not seeking anything that attracts a charge. Scans are fine. Where an item is already on Coflein, a stable reference and link is enough **provided** you confirm the online record is complete. If any item is held elsewhere — The National Archives, Glamorgan Archives, Cadw, Heneb or Amgueddfa Cymru — please name the body and reference so I can apply there directly, which I will.
>
> Finally, so that it is on record from the outset rather than raised later: please let me have the name and contact details of the officer responsible for information rights at the Commission, and confirmation of the internal review procedure, so that I know where to direct any review request if one becomes necessary.
>
> With thanks for your patience with a long list.
>
> Yn gywir / Yours faithfully,

records.transcript:
Dear Requester

Thank you for your request for an internal review of Amgueddfa Cymru's response to your Freedom of Information request concerning a reported archaeological discovery at Great House Farm, Llandough.

I have now completed my review of the handling of your request, including the searches undertaken and the concerns raised in your request for review.

Having reviewed the original request, the searches conducted and the response provided, I am satisfied that the request was handled appropriately and that reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken in those locations where information falling within the scope of the request would reasonably be expected to be held.

In your request for review, you suggest that additional searches should have been undertaken using a wider range of terms and concepts, including references to Roman burials, military burials, cavalry burials, human remains, horse remains and other archaeological terminology. I have carefully considered this point. However, when assessing whether information is held for the purposes of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, the relevant issue is not whether every conceivable search term has been used, but whether the authority has undertaken searches that are reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances and reasonably likely to identify relevant information if held.

Your request concerned a specific reported discovery at a named location. Accordingly, the location identified in the request was used as the primary search criterion. Searches were undertaken across Amgueddfa Cymru's information holdings where records relating to acquisitions, accessions, archaeological finds, provenance information and associated correspondence would reasonably be expected to be held. This included collections management systems, accession records, archived documentation, shared electronic records and other organisational record repositories.

Records identified through those searches were reviewed by collections staff and the FOI team to determine whether they related to the reported discovery described in your request. As the search methodology was location-based rather than focused on a particular object type, archaeological period or interpretation, it was reasonably likely of identifying relevant records regardless of whether associated material had been recorded as Roman, medieval or otherwise.  I have therefore considered your suggestion that later historical accounts may have inaccurately described the nature, date or attribution of the reported discovery. I am satisfied that this possibility would not have affected the outcome of the searches undertaken.

I have also considered whether broader keyword searches would have been appropriate. Given the scale and diversity of Amgueddfa Cymru's collections and records, generic terms such as "horse", "burial" or "skeleton" would retrieve large volumes of records relating to many different sites and periods and would not provide a reliable or proportionate means of locating records relating to a specific reported discovery at a named location. I am satisfied that the location-based search strategy adopted was the most appropriate and proportionate approach.

The searches undertaken did not identify any records relating to:
* the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or deposit of a visor, lance, helmet, armour or related objects associated with the discovery described in your request;
* associated human or animal remains connected with that discovery;
* reburial records relating to that discovery; or
* excavation reports, discovery reports or watching-brief records relating to the discovery described in your request.

Having reviewed both the scope of the original request and the searches undertaken, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that, if information relating to the reported discovery were held by Amgueddfa Cymru, those searches would have been likely to identify it.

You also raised concerns regarding the reference in the original response to other archaeological records identified during the course of the searches. Those records were reviewed and were not considered to relate to, or otherwise be associated with, the reported discovery described in your request. However, I can confirm that this aspect has been subject to further consideration and a separate response will be issued in relation to those records.

I therefore uphold the original conclusion that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold recorded information falling within the scope of your request.

This concludes Amgueddfa Cymru's internal review process. If you remain dissatisfied, you may complain to the Information Commissioner's Office under section 50 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

Dr Wigley,

This is a supplement to the complaint re-served on 20 September, not a
chaser. I do not expect a reply before the stage-one response. It adds
seven matters under the existing headings at section 7, and one addition to
the outcomes at section 9, set out at the end.

The public interest is engaged alongside my family's. Great House Farm
stood beside the Grade I church at Llandough, was recorded by the Royal
Commission in 1974, sat within a known archaeological site, and was
described in the post-demolition planning record as a "county treasure". I
do not ask Cadw to treat the 1994 discoveries as knowledge it had in 1988.
They show what was lost; the pre-1988 record is the measure of Cadw's
process.

On my family's account and the contemporary press report, protection was
being sought in the first days of December 1988 and the house was
demolished almost immediately afterwards. I do not ask Cadw to determine
responsibility for the demolition. The grievance is narrower: protection
was sought at the critical moment, and Cadw cannot now show what it
considered.

1. The adopted development plan (matter A)

The planning officer's report on application 89/01396/OUT records that the
supporting information to Policy H.2 of the East Vale Local Plan "states
that buildings on the site should be retained, however were unfortunately
demolished a little while ago." I do not say this bound Cadw or required
listing. I ask:
(a) was Cadw aware of it in December 1988;
(b) did the planning authority draw it to Cadw's attention; and
(c) if neither can be established, will Cadw say so expressly.

2. The search undertaken on 21 May (matters D and F)

Mr Weatherhead wrote that he had asked a colleague to search other paper
files, "including the Welsh Office files", and would write again with the
result, while fairly warning that some files had quite likely been
destroyed. I have not received that letter. Please confirm whether the
search was carried out, which series were searched, what was found, and
whether Cadw regards the ATISN 27021 response of 11 June as its report of
that search.

3. The meaning of "YYY" (matter J)

Cadw has given two accounts of the marking — that the buildings were
"marginally below the bar for listing" (21 May) and that the building did
not meet the criteria (10 July) — and one inference, that it did not meet
the criteria "as it was not included on the list" (29 July). I ask for one
settled meaning, the documentary source for it, and, if there is none, a
statement to that effect.

4. The retention period (matter J)

Your email of 27 August said that no records of the historic retention
arrangements are available, and that the three-year period is what current
colleagues advised from their knowledge of the systems then in place. I ask
only that the complaint response confirm expressly that this is an account
of general practice, not evidence that the Great House Farm file was in
fact destroyed after three years.

5. Professional archaeological knowledge of this site before December 1988
(matter C)

On 22 September 2026 Amgueddfa Cymru disclosed to me, under FOI 2026-032,
its collections records for two accessions from this site. The first,
82.44H, is the material from the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust's
excavation of 1979 on land formerly part of Great House Farm, carried out
in advance of housing development. The museum's records give the findspot
as ST 168 733, the donor as Wales & West Housing Association Ltd, and the
published report as Owen-John 1988. The accession runs to several hundred
entries and includes Roman coins, samian, glass, a bone scabbard slide and
querns, together with medieval pottery and ironwork.

This is not archaeology discovered after the event. By the time Cadw
considered this building, the site had been professionally excavated, the
finds had been accessioned by the national museum under a 1982 accession
number, and the excavation report had been published. I therefore ask, as
an addition to matter C:
(a) whether Cadw held, or had access to, the 1979 excavation record or its
published report when it considered the buildings in 1988;
(b) whether that material was drawn to its attention by GGAT, the planning
authority or the Royal Commission; and
(c) if neither can now be established, that Cadw say so in terms.

I do not say this material required the building to be listed. I say that
the conclusion recorded in December 1988, that the site was not of
sufficient archaeological interest, was reached against a professional
record that already existed and is still held by the national museum today.

6. The National Museum attribution (matter H)

The GGAT assessment of August 1990, which Cadw supplied to me on 21 May,
states that "it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the
National Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW
1988)."

The museum's disclosure allows that sentence to be tested, and the position
is more precise than either of us has previously put it. The museum does
hold medieval ironwork from this site — knife blades, arrowheads, a buckle
and a pair of compasses within accession 82.44H — but as excavated material
from 1979, not as an 1880 discovery beneath the rear wing. Its searches
found no accession, donation or deposit answering the c.1880 provenance at
all. The museum's own explanation, given in its disclosure, is that objects
recorded as found at Church Farm, Llandough in 1858 and donated in 1963
under accession 63.24 "could well be the basis for such a local
story/tradition".

I therefore no longer ask Cadw to accept that the attribution is
uncorroborated in the round. I ask, more narrowly, whether Cadw holds
anything supporting the c.1880 rear-wing provenance beyond the GGAT
sentence it forwarded, and whether it will ask that the derived record note
the museum's findings rather than continue to carry the 1880 attribution
unqualified.

7. Correcting the record (matter H)

You directed me to Heneb as manager of the HER, which was reasonable. The
only substantive reply I have had from Heneb is its statement of 22 May
that it is not subject to FOI as a limited company; a schedule I sent on 19
September remains outstanding.

The museum's disclosure now gives a firm anchor for what the record should
show. Accession 95.56H comprises the material from the Cotswold
Archaeological Trust excavation of 1994, donated by Ideal Homes Wales Ltd,
and its locality is recorded in the museum's own collections database as
"Great House Farm Llandough" at ST 1681 7331 — the grid reference carried
by the historic environment record for this site. That accession runs to
several hundred sets of early medieval human remains from this ground.

As the statutory duty to keep historic environment records rests with the
Welsh Ministers, I ask:
(a) which body is responsible for correcting an inaccurate or incomplete
historic environment record;
(b) what Cadw's own role is where the record is managed by Heneb; and
(c) what Cadw will do if the entry for this site (GGAT02038s) is not
corrected to reflect the 1979 and 1994 excavations and the accessions
arising from them.

Correction to my letter of 20 September

I said █████ had rejected my correspondence on three occasions.
Having checked properly, it rejected messages on at least eight occasions
between January and September 2026: 23 January; 9 May (twice); 17 May; 10
August; 11 August; 29 August; and 17 September. Separate failures on 29
August and 17 September came from the retired address █████.
I correct this because I have asked Cadw to distinguish what is established
from what is inferred, and the same standard applies to me.

Addition to the outcomes at section 9

6. A written acknowledgement that the 21 May undertaking was not reported
on, and that Cadw's accounts of the 1988 assessment have varied.
7. A single statement of what can and cannot now be established about the
1988 decisions, which my family can rely on and cite.
8. That Cadw write to Heneb and the Royal Commission asking that their
records for this site reflect that statement and the museum's accession
records.
9. Consideration, under the Welsh Government complaints policy, of redress
for the time and trouble my family has spent since May pursuing questions
that Cadw's own records could not answer.

I am content to supply the museum's disclosure to Cadw if that would
assist, and my offer of 20 September stands: any 1988 Cadw correspondence
recovered from the Royal Commission or Heneb will be sent to you. I remain
grateful for the courtesy you and your colleagues have shown me.

Yours sincerely,

Requester
